standard.title: Construct evidence-based arguments
standard.description: construct evidence-based arguments to support conclusions or evaluate claims and consider any ethical issues and cultural protocols associated with using or citing secondary data or information
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can compare methods, recognise sources of error and select evidence to draw reasoned conclusions (AC9S5I05). They have not yet constructed arguments with explicit evidence-reasoning structure or considered ethical issues around using secondary data.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students construct evidence-based arguments to support conclusions or evaluate claims, considering ethical issues and cultural protocols associated with using or citing secondary data or information.

nodes.label: Drawing conclusions from evidence
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can draw a conclusion from evidence that supports or rejects a hypothesis and identify the evidence used
nodes.minimum_width: Draw a conclusion from evidence that supports or rejects a hypothesis; identify the evidence used
nodes.typical_width: Draw a logical conclusion considering the method of data collection, quality of evidence and limitations or significance of a claim
wider: Draw conclusions from an investigation where the evidence is ambiguous and explain why the conclusion is uncertain
Compare two investigations that reach different conclusions about the same question and explain what accounts for the difference
Evaluate whether a conclusion is justified by the evidence or whether it over-reaches

response_modes.reason: Students commonly state conclusions without identifying the specific evidence that supports them, or over-reach beyond what the evidence shows. Scaffolding the conclusion-drawing process — what evidence do I have, what does it show, does it support or reject the hypothesis, and what are its limits — builds the explicit connection between evidence and conclusion that the descriptor requires.

success_criteria: Draws a conclusion that is consistent with the evidence
Identifies the specific evidence that supports the conclusion
States whether the evidence supports or rejects the hypothesis

nodes.label: Constructing evidence-based arguments
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can construct an argument supported by evidence and reasoning to support a conclusion or evaluate a claim
nodes.minimum_width: Construct an argument that links evidence to a conclusion with reasoning; evaluate one claim by assessing the evidence behind it
nodes.typical_width: Construct arguments supported by evidence and reasoning to support or reject a hypothesis; evaluate the credibility of sources; assess whether cited evidence is sufficient to support a claim
wider: Evaluate a contested scientific claim by systematically assessing the credibility, relevance and sufficiency of evidence from multiple sources
Investigate cultural, historical and archaeological evidence used in the scientific debate about the role of early First Nations Australians in the extinction of Australian megafauna
Construct competing arguments for and against a claim and evaluate which is better supported

response_modes.reason: Students commonly state conclusions and list evidence without connecting them through reasoning — the 'because' is missing. Constructing arguments across different science content areas (ecology, forces, classification, megafauna extinction) helps students practise the evidence-reasoning-conclusion structure rather than relying on the familiarity of one context to carry the argument.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The megafauna extinction direction is genuinely rich — it involves multiple evidence types (cultural, historical, archaeological, ecological), contested interpretations, and the intersection of First Nations knowledge with Western scientific methods. Advancing students who investigate this case encounter a real scientific debate where argument quality is actively tested, not a textbook example with a settled answer.
success_criteria: Constructs an argument that links evidence to a conclusion through reasoning
The reasoning explains why the evidence supports the conclusion
Does not simply list evidence without connecting it to the conclusion

nodes.label: Ethics of using secondary data
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can consider ethical issues and cultural protocols associated with using or citing secondary data or information
nodes.minimum_width: Identify one ethical issue or cultural protocol relevant to using secondary data; explain why it matters
nodes.typical_width: Consider ethical issues and cultural protocols when using secondary data from First Nations Australians or other culturally sensitive sources; evaluate the credibility and appropriateness of citing secondary sources
wider: Research the development of commercial products founded on traditional knowledges of First Nations Australians and discuss ethical considerations around biopiracy and intellectual property rights
Evaluate a case where secondary data was used without appropriate cultural protocols and explain the consequences
Develop a set of criteria for ethically using and citing secondary data from culturally sensitive sources

response_modes.reason: Students commonly identify ethical issues as abstract principles without reasoning through the specific consequences — they name 'biopiracy' without explaining what harm occurs, to whom, and why the protocol exists. Scaffolding the reasoning (whose knowledge is this, what are the ownership rights, what protocol applies, and what happens if it's violated?) makes the ethical consideration concrete and actionable.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The biopiracy and intellectual property direction is rich — it connects to real current debates about Indigenous knowledge rights, patent law, and benefit-sharing agreements. Advancing students who investigate specific cases (e.g. commercial products derived from traditional plant knowledge) engage with genuinely complex ethical territory that goes well beyond academic citation ethics.
success_criteria: Identifies an ethical issue or cultural protocol relevant to using secondary data
Explains why the issue matters for the integrity of the argument
Recognises that cultural knowledge requires specific protocols for use and citation
